notes.text: Luxembourg has one of the most rate-sensitive mortgage flows in the euro area: ECB data show that loans at a floating rate or with an initial rate fixation of up to one year made up between about 36% and 51% of new house-purchase lending in the months reported for 2025 and 52% in June 2026, against about 17% for the euro area in August 2026. ECB cuts and hikes therefore pass quickly into borrowing costs, making the market unusually responsive to the policy cycle.

notes.text: Since 1 January 2021, and as of its 2020 notification, the CSSF has applied legally binding loan-to-value limits on new residential mortgages: 100% for first-time buyers of a primary residence, 90% for other primary-residence buyers with 15% of such lending allowed up to 100%, and 80% for other loans including buy-to-let. The limits were introduced to curb the combination of high household debt and high prices, and the tighter 80% cap restrains leveraged investor purchases most.

notes.text: Buyers of a home they will occupy as their main residence can offset the 7% registration and transcription duties with the Bëllegen Akt tax credit, which the 2024 housing package raised from EUR 30,000 to EUR 40,000 per buyer for deeds signed between 1 January 2024 and 30 June 2025; bill 8540 proposed keeping the higher cap permanently for deeds from 1 July 2025. At 7%, a EUR 40,000 credit covers the duties on roughly EUR 570,000 of price per buyer, lowering entry costs for owner-occupiers, and part of that support is likely to be capitalised into prices.
